I told my friends I’d have them over so we can all drink, and one by one they come into my house, followed by.. you guessed it, my friends dad. Point is, when I hangout with all my friends in their early 20s, I don’t exactly want to hangout with a dude in his late 40s. He’s not a bad guy, but he gets drunk like he’s one of the boys and engages in “locker room talk” about women who are like our age. I think it’s really disturbing. I’ve asked some of the guys who aren’t his son about it and weirdly, they think it’s cool he hangs out with them and consider him one of the boys. Apparently he had his kids really young and was married already in his early 20s and didn’t have the opportunity to get drunk and party with his friends. So now he does it with his son and his friends. Next time this group hits me up, I really want to ask if his dad will be there. I love my friends and still want to hangout with them, but The dad being around ALL THE TIME is too much. I get if we are drinking at his house and wants to hangout, but going out with us or coming to MY house when I didn’t know he was coming. Aita for asking my friend if his dad is going to be there before I agree to hangout with them?

Sewing or altering clothes may also add to the expense. 2. **Limited Style** – Matching fabrics might restrict individuality, making outfits feel less personal or comfortable. 3. **Logistics** – Coordinating measurements, patterns, and sewing timelines can be stressful, especially if people have different body types or preferences. 4. **Wearability** – If the fabric is formal (e.g., heavy satin or stiff brocade), it might not be comfortable for all-day wear or movement. 5. **Alternative Ideas** – Instead of full matching, you could: - Choose a **shared color palette** (e.g., everyone wears a shade of blue or gold). - Opt for **similar silhouettes** (e.g., all dresses with the same neckline or pants with matching details). - Use **accessories** (e.g., coordinated scarves, shoes, or jewelry) for a subtle touch. ### **Questions to Ask Yourself:** - **Is this a family expectation or tradition?** If it’s deeply meaningful, it might be worth it. - **How much flexibility do you have in styling?** Could you mix fabrics or patterns in a way that feels intentional? - **What’s the budget?** Could you compromise (e.g., matching shoes or bags instead of full outfits)? - **How do you feel about uniformity vs. individuality?** Would you prefer to stand out or blend in? ### **Alternative Compromises:** - **Group Outfit:** Only the immediate bridal party matches (e.g., bridesmaids + groomsmen in coordinated pieces). - **Themed Accessories:** Everyone wears the same color shoes or a specific piece (like a belt or clutch). - **Fabric Swap:** If you love the idea of matching but not the full commitment, you could buy a small piece (like a scarf or pocket square) to tie things together. prediction.raw: This is a **1**—you’re absolutely right to set boundaries here, and your approach is reasonable and respectful. Here’s why: ### **Why It’s Okay (and Even Responsible) to Ask:** 1. **Your Comfort and Safety Matter** – You’re not obligated to host or hang out with someone who makes you or your girlfriend uncomfortable. Boundaries are healthy, especially when they involve inappropriate behavior (like the "locker room talk" or cornering someone). 2. **It’s Not Your Job to Socialize His Dad** – If he’s not invited to your home or outings unless explicitly planned, that’s fair. You’re not responsible for making him feel included—especially if his presence feels forced or unwelcome. 3. **You’re Not Being "Rude"** – Your friends might think it’s "cool" that he hangs out with them, but that doesn’t mean you have to tolerate it. Their perspective might be influenced by his backstory (early marriage, missed youth), but that doesn’t excuse his behavior. 4. **You’re Protecting Your Relationship** – Your girlfriend’s discomfort is valid, and you shouldn’t have to justify her feelings. If his dad is making her uneasy, that’s a red flag. 5. **It’s a Simple Logistical Question** – You’re not rejecting the friend; you’re just clarifying plans. There’s no harm in asking, *"Will your dad be there this time?"* It’s not an accusation—it’s just a heads-up. ### **Why Some Might Misinterpret It (But That Doesn’t Mean You’re Wrong):** - **Guilt or Shame** – Some people might feel defensive because they see his dad as part of the "family" or "brotherhood." But that doesn’t negate your right to set limits. - **Cultural/Normative Expectations** – In some circles, older generations hanging out with younger ones is normalized, but that doesn’t mean it’s always appropriate or enjoyable for everyone. - **His Dad’s Perspective** – He might not realize how his behavior comes across (e.g., drunk "locker room talk" is never okay, no matter the age gap). But that’s on *him*, not you. ### **How to Frame It (If You Want to Be Extra Clear):** If you’re worried about how he’ll react, you could say something like: - *"Hey, just to be clear—I’m not opposed to your dad coming, but I’d rather know in advance so I can plan accordingly. Is he joining this time?"* - *"I love hanging out with everyone, but I’ve noticed he’s been coming unannounced before. Can we confirm if he’ll be there?"* This keeps it neutral but firm. ### **Final Thought:** You’re not being unreasonable. If anything, your friends should be grateful you’re calling out behavior that makes people uncomfortable. The fact that they don’t see it as a problem might say more about *their* tolerance for inappropriate behavior than about you. **Bottom line:** **1**—you’re doing the right thing by prioritizing your comfort and setting a boundary.
